title: Psenicska v. Twentieth Century Fox Film Corp. — appeal
lead: Participants who said they had been recruited for a documentary challenged the releases they signed before appearing in Borat. Their appeals turned on the meaning of documentary style and whether specific nonreliance clauses defeated the fraud-based route around those releases.

actors.name: Michael Psenicska
actors.role: Driving instructor filmed giving Borat a lesson

actors.name: Cindy Streit and dinner guests
actors.role: Participants in a filmed etiquette dinner

actors.name: Twentieth Century Fox and associated filmmakers

proceedings: Judge Preska dismissed three related actions under Rule 12(b)(6). A Second Circuit panel reviewed anew and affirmed the September 24, 2008 judgment dismissing all three.
limits: The courts assumed pleaded facts for dismissal and did not find the alleged deception untrue. The appellate analysis of peculiar knowledge belongs to this separate November 17, 2009 decision, not retroactively to the district court.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with the complete effective canonical brief; no new independent opinion verification claimed.

sections.title: The production recruited instructors and dinner guests
sections.cue: Introduce the people and their alleged expectations.
paragraphs: Michael Psenicska had operated a driving school for thirty-two years. He alleged that Todd Lewis Schulman contacted him in May 2005 about a documentary concerning foreign people's integration into American life. He agreed to meet the crew in Washington, D.C., on June 13 but said he had to leave by 5 p.m. for a 6 p.m. class. The crew allegedly arrived ninety minutes late, paid $500, and presented unexpected papers described as necessary for the documentary. Rushed and without his reading glasses, Psenicska signed without reading, relying on their earlier conversations. Sacha Baron Cohen, playing Borat, then allegedly drove erratically and made derogatory remarks. Psenicska accused people he believed were producers of setting him up and later unsuccessfully sought an explanation from Schulman.

Cindy Streit owned an etiquette-training business called ETS. She alleged that Schulman requested training and a dinner for a Belarus dignitary in an educational documentary for Belarus television. Streit and Springland Films signed a services contract on October 24, 2005. The arrangements changed so Borat would skip instruction but attend the dinner. Guests included Sarah Moseley, Ben McKinnon, Michael Jared, and Lynn Jared. According to the plaintiffs, the crew arrived late and rushed them to review consent forms just before Borat arrived; each signed. They alleged sexist remarks and introduction of a woman as a prostitute. The film showed some guests leaving and portrayed Borat implying that they were racially intolerant. After filming but before suit, Streit, ETS and Springland signed a separate liability release: Streit received $4,450 for releasing her and ETS's claims against Springland and related entities. That later release was not the common ground for dismissal of all three lawsuits.

Kathie Martin operated the Etiquette Training School of Birmingham. She alleged an arrangement for dining instruction to a foreign reporter filmed for Belarus television. When Schulman learned that Martin's husband knew another Cohen character from Da Ali G Show, he allegedly postponed filming to reduce the chance of recognition. At the rescheduled meeting Martin received $350 and signed what Schulman called a standard filming release. Cohen allegedly made sexist and anti-Semitic comments and displayed nude photographs of his supposed son. The director apologized for the photographs; Martin's husband later identified Cohen, and Martin unsuccessfully tried to reach Schulman. These were participation allegations, not findings after trial.

sections.title: Signed agreements controlled the dismissal motions
sections.cue: Explain the release and the attempted escape from it.
paragraphs: Psenicska sued on December 3, 2007. The Streit plaintiffs sued in Alabama, and their case was transferred to the Southern District of New York in February 2008. Martin filed in February 2008. Claims included fraud, unjust enrichment and emotional distress. Their materially identical Standard Consent Agreements authorized a documentary-style motion picture for a young-adult audience using entertaining content and formats. Psenicska's named One America; the others named Springland. They waived participation claims including publicity or likeness, intrusion, prima facie tort, and fraud involving deception or surprise about the film or agreement. Martin's also specifically covered sexually oriented materials or activities. Paragraph 5 separately disclaimed reliance on statements about the film's nature and identities of participants or creators.

Judge Loretta A. Preska granted all three Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal motions on September 3, 2008, directed closure of the actions, and denied pending motions as moot. She accepted material allegations as true and could consider the agreements incorporated in or relied upon by the complaints. Under the undisputed New York choice-of-law clause, ambiguity was a legal question. A documentary-style fictional journey could include real interviews and events, and humor did not disqualify it. Paragraph 5 was a targeted nonreliance provision, not merely a general merger clause: it defeated the attempted fraud-based escape from the releases. Recasting the same asserted misunderstanding as nondisclosure did not supply reliance. Having resolved those grounds, she did not reach every other defense.

On appeal, Judges Roger J. Miner, John M. Walker Jr., and Reena Raggi reviewed the dismissals anew, accepting allegations and reasonable favorable inferences. The judgment under review was dated September 24, 2008. They considered whether ambiguity or fraudulent inducement prevented enforcement, rather than determining that the alleged misrepresentations never happened. Their fuller peculiar-knowledge analysis belonged to this appeal, not retroactively to Preska's memorandum.

sections.title: A fictional visitor could appear in documentary style
sections.cue: Explain why the genre argument did not create ambiguity.
paragraphs: The plaintiffs argued that documentary style did not clearly authorize their appearances in Borat. The panel treated ambiguity as a legal question and concluded that no reasonable factfinder could place this film outside the phrase.

Borat was fictional, but his story unmistakably used traditional documentary presentation, including real interviews and events. The contrast between those encounters and the fictional visitor was itself a comic device. Truth of the story and style of presentation were different questions. Even if other productions might fall near an uncertain genre boundary, this film comfortably fit the description. Ambiguity therefore did not prevent enforcement at the pleading stage.

sections.title: The disclaimer addressed the very subjects of alleged fraud
sections.cue: Explain the peculiar-knowledge exception and its limits.
paragraphs: New York fraudulent-inducement law required reasonable reliance. Under Danann, the precedent addressing specific nonreliance provisions, a party generally could not base inducement on representations about a subject expressly disclaimed in the contract. Paragraph 5 targeted precisely the nature of the film and the people involved.

The plaintiffs invoked an exception for facts peculiarly within the alleged wrongdoer’s knowledge. The panel explained that the exception protects against high costs of determining whether an oral assertion is true; it ordinarily does not protect someone able to demand that a deal-breaking assurance be written into the agreement.

The plaintiffs apparently took no confirming steps, such as asking the reporter’s name or requesting to meet him. More fundamentally, they identified no collateral harm from declining participation if the filmmakers refused satisfactory written assurances. They could make their asserted conditions part of the bargain or walk away. Signing a writing disclaiming those representations and then invoking them as fraud did not fit the exception.

The panel expressly withheld approval of the alleged conduct if true. Its conclusion neither declared the filmmakers honest nor abolished protection where information is genuinely inaccessible or costly to obtain. It enforced these releases on these allegations.

sections.title: Recasting the statements as omissions did not supply reliance
sections.cue: State the final affirmance and its reach.
paragraphs: The plaintiffs also alleged a duty to disclose the truth. But concealment and disclosure-based theories required reasonable reliance too. Nothing written promised a documentary about a foreign visitor for Belarus television. That understanding arose from the oral statements on which the plaintiffs had specifically disclaimed reliance. Describing the same misunderstanding as an omission did not cure the defect.

On November 17, 2009, after rejecting the remaining arguments, the panel affirmed the September 24, 2008 judgment dismissing all three complaints. No judge wrote separately. It ordered no damages, factual hearing, or renegotiation, leaving these releases enforceable against the claims without adjudicating the truth of the alleged deception.
